stories.title: At least 15 die as boat sinks in Zimbabwe's Lake Kariba
stories.summary: The vessel is said to have overturned after being hit by strong waves.
stories.post: 📰 NEWS: At least 15 die as boat sinks in Zimbabwe's Lake Kariba. The vessel is said to have overturned after being hit by strong waves. Source: BBC World.
article_sentences: Police said 90 passengers and five crew were onboard the vessel when it capsized on Tuesday, but it may have been overloaded, with other reports pointing to a higher number based on the registered ticket sales.
The vessel was hit by a strong wave and overturned, police added.
Footage shared online appears to show the hull floating in the water.
Lake Kariba, which straddles the border with Zambia, is one of the world's largest man-made reservoirs, supporting transport and fishing and providing vital hydroelectric power to both countries.
The Zimbabwe's Civil Protection Unit (CPU) said that registered ticket sales showed 114 adults were on board the vessel.
There could also have been an unknown number of children below ticketing age, it added.
"So far, 77 passengers have been rescued by Matusadonha rescue teams and others," the CPU said.
It added that "15 bodies have also been retrieved", and two funeral parlours had been engaged to collect the bodies for processing.

Mutsa Murombedzi, a local member of parliament, posted a video on X, externalof what she said was the boat at the start of the journey, adding that locals had been using it to travel across the lake to Kariba town, a journey that takes about five hours.
"We have very hard questions that require honest answers.
The officials must release the correct number of people who were onboard," she wrote.
Police said more details would be released "in due course".

stories.title: What can we learn from eclipses?
stories.summary: A total solar eclipse will sweep across northern Spain on August 12 in one of Europe's most anticipated astronomical events of the decade. From the Sun's corona to animal behaviour and human emotions, these rare celestial events continue to provide scientists with valuable insights more than two millennia after they were first observed. Head of Space Science at the Centre National d'Études Spatiales, Olivier Joie-La Marle, shares further insights.
